stops.title: Junction City
story: All aboard! Welcome to the Utah Depot. Every week, our train stops somewhere in Utah, and we learn a true story about what happened there. Our first stop is home: Union Station in Ogden.

The railroad first came to Ogden in 1869. The Union Pacific laid its tracks down through Weber Canyon and into town. Brigham Young set aside land in Ogden for railroad yards, the places where trains are parked, sorted and fixed. With trains coming and going, Ogden got a nickname that stuck: Junction City. A junction is a place where railroads meet.

That same year, something big happened just northwest of Ogden, at a place called Promontory Summit. Two railroad companies had been racing to build one railroad across the whole country. The Central Pacific built east from Sacramento, California. The Union Pacific built west from Omaha, Nebraska. On May 10, 1869, their tracks finally met.

The two engines, the Central Pacific's Jupiter and the Union Pacific's No. 119, pulled up face to face, with just one rail's width between them. A golden spike was part of the ceremony. Here's a funny part: Leland Stanford and Thomas Durant, two of the railroad leaders, each swung a hammer at the spike, and each one missed!
The spike and hammer were wired to the telegraph so the whole country could hear the news. Then a telegraph operator sent one word: "done."

Ogden's train station has its own story. In 1923, a fire almost destroyed it. A new station was finished in 1924, built right on the old foundation. You can still visit it today on 25th Street. Inside are museums, including the Utah State Railroad Museum.
Now our engine is ready to roll. The tracks split three ways. Where should the Utah Depot go next?

quiz.why: A junction is a place where railroads meet.

quiz.q: The two railroads met at Promontory Summit in 1969.
Union Station was rebuilt after a fire.
quiz.why: It burned in 1923 and was rebuilt in 1924.

stops.draw: Draw the two engines, Jupiter and No. 119, nose to nose at Promontory Summit.
stops.find: Visit Union Station on 25th Street in Ogden and find the Utah State Railroad Museum. Or ask a grandparent: did you ever ride a train?

word.def: A place where two or more roads or railroads meet. Can you find a junction near your house?

stops.math: If the train goes 40 miles an hour, how long would a trip to Golden Spike take? (Hint: it's 40 miles away.)

stops.title: Golden Spike
story: All aboard! Our train rolled about 40 miles northwest from Ogden, around the north side of the Great Salt Lake, to Promontory Summit. This is the spot where the two railroads met in 1869. Today it is Golden Spike National Historical Park.

Last stop, we learned that the Central Pacific built east from California and the Union Pacific built west from Nebraska. Building a railroad took thousands of workers. The Central Pacific started by hiring 50 Chinese workers. They were so strong and hardworking that the company hired many more. About 10,000 Chinese workers helped build the railroad.

The work was hard and dangerous. More than one thousand Chinese workers likely died building the Central Pacific. On June 24, 1867, Chinese workers in the mountains of California stopped work together. It was the largest organized workers' strike in the country at that time.

Near the end, the two railroads made a bet: who could lay the most track in one day? On April 28, 1869, the Central Pacific went for 10 miles. At sunrise, eight Irish track layers started moving the heavy rails into place. Behind them, at least 400 Chinese workers laid the wooden ties, spiked the rails down, bolted them together and packed the ground under the track.
When the sun went down, they had laid 10 miles and 56 feet of track in a single day. That beat the Union Pacific by almost 2 miles!
Twelve days later, on May 10, 1869, eight Chinese workers set the very last rail into place. The last tie was made of polished laurel wood, with holes drilled for the special spikes.

If you visit the park today, you can see working copies of the two engines, Jupiter and No. 119. They came to the park in 1979, 110 years after the tracks first met. Toot toot! Next week, Timmy the Tyrannosaurus is taking the train to Dinosaur Park. All aboard!

quiz.q: About 10,000 Chinese workers helped build the Central Pacific Railroad.
quiz.why: They did much of the hardest work, from the mountains of California to Utah.

quiz.q: On the 10-mile day, the workers laid 10 miles of track in one week.
quiz.why: It was one day: April 28, 1869. They laid 10 miles and 56 feet!

quiz.q: The last tie at Promontory was made of laurel wood.
quiz.why: It was a polished laurel wood tie with holes drilled for the spikes.

stops.draw: Draw the workers on the 10-mile day: someone carrying a rail, someone hammering a spike, and the sun going down.
stops.find: Go outside and count your steps for one minute. The 10-mile day was about 21,000 steps for a grown-up! Or visit Golden Spike National Historical Park with a grown-up and see Jupiter and No. 119.

word.def: A railroad tie is the wooden board that goes across the ground under the rails. The rails are spiked to the ties. Can you find something at home made of wood boards?

stops.math: The workers laid 10 miles in one day. How many miles would they lay in 3 days at that speed?

ticketBook.secretFact: Secret caboose fact: Ogden's 1924 Union Station was designed by John and Donald Parkinson in a style called Spanish Colonial Revival. It was built in 1924 on the foundation of the station that burned.
